answer_1.quote: Hallucinations in machine translation (MT) are cases when the model generates output that is partially or fully unrelated to the source sentence.

answer_2.quote: We use: • chrF: character n-gram F score of the translation with respect to the reference. We use the CHRF++ version that also takes into account word unigrams and bigrams (Popović, 2017); • COMET: a neural quality estimation metric by  which was shown to be the state-of-the-art reference-based method.

answer_4.quote: We perform a human evaluation. With each method, we translate the same 200 source sentences. They are randomly sampled from the hallucination dataset... The 602 resulting sentence pairs are labeled by 3 annotators into three categories: Correct, Error, and Hallucination.
answer_4.guideline: Annotators were provided with the guidelines shown in Table . For the reporting purposes, 'Partial hallucination' was grouped together with 'Full hallucination', and 'Undertranslation' with 'Other'.
criteria: OK: An acceptable translation; it conveys the main meaning correctly and does not introduce extra meaning.
Partial hallucination: a part of the translation is unrelated to the source, or is related very indirectly
Full hallucination: most or all of the translation is unrelated to the source
Undertranslation: there is no hallucinations, but a significant part of the source is not translated at all
Other: there are no hallucinations or undertranlsations, but there are other translation errors that make the translation unacceptable.
